title: WHY WOULD GOD SEND EZEKIEL TO PEOPLE HE ALREADY KNEW WOULDN’T LISTEN?
paragraphs: WHY WOULD GOD SEND EZEKIEL TO PEOPLE HE ALREADY KNEW WOULDN’T LISTEN?
The frightening answer is not really about Ezekiel. It is about what God does when people keep hearing His voice… while quietly deciding they will not obey.
Imagine being called by God to preach a message that almost nobody wants.
Not because you are unclear.
Not because you lack passion.
Not because you chose the wrong words.
God Himself tells you beforehand that the people probably will not listen.
Would you still go?
Would you keep speaking after the tenth rejection?
After the hundredth?
Would you remain faithful when there were no applause, no visible results, no dramatic testimonies proving that your obedience was “working”?
That was Ezekiel's assignment.
And hidden inside that painful assignment is one of the most uncomfortable truths in Scripture:
Sometimes the success of obedience is not measured by whether people respond.
Sometimes success is simply that God spoke…
and His servant refused to remain silent.

Ezekiel was among the Jewish exiles in Babylon after Judah's rebellion had brought devastating judgment. He was not preaching to people who had never heard about the God of Israel. He was speaking to covenant people—people surrounded by the history, promises, warnings, and revelation of God.
And God told him something devastating.
In Ezekiel 3:7, the Hebrew reads:
וּבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יֹאבוּ לִשְׁמֹעַ אֵלֶיךָ כִּי־אֵינָם אֹבִים לִשְׁמֹעַ אֵלָי
Uveit Yisra'el lo yovu lishmoa elekha, ki-einam ovim lishmoa elai…
The force of the statement is chilling:
Israel will not be willing to listen to you…
because they are not willing to listen to Me.
That changes everything.
Ezekiel's rejection was not ultimately about Ezekiel.
God was exposing the deeper rebellion beneath it.
The people had a listening problem because they had a surrender problem.
And suddenly this ancient scene beside the Chebar River feels frighteningly modern.
Because you can listen to sermons without listening to God.
You can highlight Bible verses without surrendering to the God who spoke them.

You can repost Christian content, sing worship songs, attend church, know theological vocabulary, argue doctrine, say “Amen,” and still protect one locked room inside your heart where Jesus is not allowed to rule.
There is hearing with the ears.
And then there is hearing that bows.
That distinction appears throughout Scripture.
Jesus would later say:

“He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
(Matthew 11:15)
The issue was never merely whether sound entered someone's ears.
The question was whether truth entered deeply enough to produce repentance, faith, and obedience.
And this is where Ezekiel becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“Why did God send Ezekiel to people who wouldn't listen?”
Perhaps the question has become:
How many times has God spoken to me while I pretended not to understand because obedience would cost me something?
Sit with that.
Maybe you knew you needed to forgive.
But resentment felt safer.
Maybe you knew the relationship was pulling you away from Christ.
But loneliness frightened you more than compromise.
Maybe God exposed the pornography.
The secret messages.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The dishonesty.
The obsession with money.
The need for approval.
The hidden double life nobody at church knows about.
And instead of saying, “Lord, change me,” you became skilled at saying:
“I'll deal with it later.”
That is one of the terrifying possibilities raised by Ezekiel.
A heart does not normally become hard overnight.
It becomes hard through repeated resistance.
One ignored conviction at a time.
One defended sin at a time.
One excuse at a time.
One “tomorrow” at a time.
Until eventually a person can sit beneath truth…
feel almost nothing…
and call the absence of conviction peace.
God described Ezekiel's audience as stubborn of heart and hard of forehead. The Hebrew expression in Ezekiel 3:7 includes:
חִזְקֵי־מֵצַח וּקְשֵׁי־לֵב
chizkei-metzach u'qeshei-lev—
strong or hardened of forehead, and hard of heart.
This was defiance.
The posture of someone who has planted his feet and effectively said:
“I heard You.
But I still want my way.”
Yet here is the astonishing thing.
God still sent Ezekiel.
Think about what that means.
God knew their resistance…
and sent a messenger anyway.
He knew some would reject the warning…
and warned them anyway.
He knew hearts were hard…
and spoke anyway.
Why?
Because divine warning is itself an expression of divine mercy.
Judgment without warning would leave no prophetic alarm.
But God raised a watchman.

Ezekiel 3 describes that responsibility. The prophet was appointed as a watchman who had to warn the wicked. Ezekiel could not control whether someone repented. He could control whether he faithfully delivered what God entrusted to him.
That distinction matters enormously.
God did not tell Ezekiel:
“Make them repent.”
He told him, in essence:
Speak My words.
The results belonged to God.
The obedience belonged to Ezekiel.
Somebody reading this needs that truth.
You have been praying for a child who seems farther from God than ever.
Keep praying.
You have spoken truth lovingly to someone who brushed it aside.
Keep loving.
You have shared the Gospel and wondered whether a single word mattered.
Remain faithful.
You have tried to raise your family around Christ while watching culture preach another gospel every hour of every day.
Remain faithful.
Faithfulness is not failure simply because you cannot immediately see fruit.
Seeds disappear beneath dirt before anyone sees life.
But Ezekiel's story contains another side that cannot be softened.
The hearer also bears responsibility.
By Ezekiel 33, something almost haunting happens.
People come to hear Ezekiel.
They sit before him.
They listen.
They apparently find him compelling.
Yet God says they hear his words…
but do not do them.
The Hebrew is painfully direct:
וְשָׁמְעוּ אֶת־דְּבָרֶיךָ וְאוֹתָם לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ
vesham'u et-devarekha, ve'otam lo ya'asu.
They hear your words…
but they will not do them.
Ezekiel had effectively become religious content.
Something to hear.
Something to discuss.
Something compelling enough to attract attention…
but not authoritative enough, in their hearts, to interrupt their lives.
And if that does not frighten the modern church, perhaps it should.
Because we live in an age with more Christian content available in a person's pocket than generations before us could have imagined.
Sermons.
Podcasts.
Bible apps.
Devotionals.
Christian reels.
Prophecy videos.
Worship playlists.
Bible studies.
Books.
Clips.
Quotes.
Millions upon millions of words about God.
Yet information about God is not the same thing as transformation by God.
You can consume Christian content until midnight and still refuse Christ the moment obedience becomes expensive.
You can know Greek words and still refuse forgiveness.
You can study Hebrew and still hide adultery.
You can defend biblical morality publicly while nurturing secret sin privately.
You can win theological arguments while losing tenderness toward Jesus.
Knowledge can tell you what repentance means.
Only surrender actually repents.
And this is precisely where Ezekiel's message must lead us beyond Ezekiel.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible's story is not ultimately about humanity learning to behave better.
It is the story of sinners who desperately need rescue.
The prophets warned.
Humanity rebelled.
God called.
Humanity wandered.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until the One to whom the prophets ultimately point stepped into our world.
Jesus did not come merely carrying another warning.
He came bringing Himself.

The eternal Son of God entered human history, lived without sin, proclaimed the kingdom of God, called sinners to repentance and faith, went willingly to the cross, bore judgment for sinners, died, was buried, and rose again.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people eventually earned God's acceptance.
The scandal is grace.
Christ died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not once we became impressive.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not when our record finally became clean.
While sinners.
At the cross, human rebellion met divine mercy.
The holy judgment our sin deserves and the astonishing love of God are not enemies there.
They meet in Jesus.
And suddenly the question changes again.
Why would God keep speaking to people who would not listen?
Why warn rebels?
Why pursue wanderers?
Why call sinners to repent?
Why send prophets?
Why send apostles?
Why preserve His Word?
Why proclaim the Gospel?
Because God's patience should never be mistaken for indifference.
His warnings are invitations to turn before judgment.
And ultimately, He sent His Son.
Maybe you have ignored God for years.
Maybe you know exactly how to appear Christian.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe nobody knows what you deleted.
Maybe nobody knows what addiction keeps winning.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is healthy.
Maybe everybody thinks your faith is strong.
Maybe you have become so good at smiling that even you sometimes forget how tired you are.
But Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel calls you.
Not deeper into pretending.
Out of hiding.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up enough to approach Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who alone can save.
Grace does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters terribly.
Grace says your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
That is why our heartbeat remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Peter had denial in his story.
Jesus was not finished.
Paul had persecution in his story.
Jesus was not finished.
The thief beside Christ had a ruined life and almost no time left.
Jesus was not finished.
And if you are breathing while reading this…
your story is not finished either.
But do not turn that into permission to delay.
Grace is not permission to keep running from God.
Grace is the reason you can finally stop running.
There is something else extraordinary in Ezekiel's commission.
Before Ezekiel was told to speak God's Word, he was commanded to consume the scroll.
The message had to enter him before it came through him.
That is a word desperately needed in an age obsessed with broadcasting.
Before asking, “What can I post?”
Ask:
“What is God changing in me?”
Before preaching repentance to everybody else…
repent.
Before telling the world to surrender…
surrender.
Before exposing everybody else's darkness…
bring your own darkness into Christ's light.
The world does not merely need louder Christians.
It needs faithful Christians.
Christians whose private lives increasingly agree with their public confession.
Christians who love truth more than applause.
Christians who can speak without needing immediate validation.
Christians who remember that the Gospel is not a brand.
Jesus is Lord.
And perhaps this explains another part of Ezekiel's calling.
God made Ezekiel resilient.
The people were hard, so the prophet would need holy endurance—not cruelty, not arrogance, not emotional numbness, but a God-given steadfastness that would keep him obedient when rejection arrived.
Because rejection can corrupt a messenger too.
When people refuse truth, we can become bitter.
When they mock faith, we can become cruel.
When they reject Christ, we can begin treating them like enemies instead of people desperately needing Him.
But Jesus shows another way.
Truth without compromise.
Grace without pretending sin is harmless.
Conviction without hatred.
Compassion without surrendering holiness.
The cross destroys both our self-righteousness and our hopelessness.
You cannot stand beneath the cross believing you saved yourself.
And you cannot honestly stand beneath the cross believing God has no mercy for repentant sinners.
So perhaps Ezekiel was sent to people who would not listen because God's Word needed to stand among them as witness.
Perhaps because some would eventually remember.
Perhaps because the responsibility of the watchman was faithfulness rather than manipulation.
Perhaps because God's holiness required truth to be spoken.
And perhaps because warning rebellious people demonstrates something astonishing about God's character:
He speaks even when sinners resist Him.
That should break something open inside us.
Because some of us are alive spiritually today because God did not stop at our first “no.”
Or our tenth.
Someone kept praying.
Someone kept preaching.
Someone kept loving.
Someone handed us Scripture.
Someone invited us again.
Some sermon followed us home.
Some verse would not leave us alone.
Some midnight collapse finally made the truth we had resisted become the truth we desperately needed.
God's Word kept knocking against the walls we built.
Until grace found us standing in the wreckage of our own rebellion.
So now I need to ask you something personal.
Not as content.
Not as religious entertainment.
What has God already told you that you keep refusing to obey?
You probably do not need another hundred sermons about it.
You may already know.
Forgive them.
End the affair.
Confess the lie.
Leave the secret sin.
Come back to prayer.
Open Scripture again.
Stop worshiping people's approval.
Stop pretending.
Ask for help.
Return to Christ.
Repent.
Trust Him.
Maybe your heart is whispering, “Later.”
Ezekiel's generation teaches us why “later” is dangerous.
Repeated resistance has consequences.
Do not confuse God's patience with God's approval.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can mark this moment honestly.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches ruined places.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose name came into your mind while reading this.
The child drifting from God.
The friend hiding behind humor.
The believer slowly becoming cold.
The person everybody thinks is okay.

It does not. We glorify God through Christ-centered faith and obedient lives, not through transactions or social-media metrics. But sharing biblical truth can become one small act of witness when the motive is love: “Someone in my world needs to hear this.”
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that rejection does not make faithfulness meaningless…
and failure does not make redemption impossible.

Supporting a ministry is not a way to purchase God's blessing, prove your salvation, or earn His favor; salvation is God's gift of grace in Christ. But believers who freely choose to support Gospel work can do so as an act of generosity and partnership in spreading biblical truth.
Listen to Jesus.
Not merely with your ears.
With your life.
Because one day Ezekiel's audience discovered something terrifying:
The prophet they treated like entertainment had been telling them the truth.
Do not wait until consequences teach you what Scripture was already trying to tell you through mercy.
God sent Ezekiel even though people would refuse to listen.
And centuries later, God sent His Son into a world that would reject Him.
They mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Beat Him.
Crucified Him.
And from the place that looked like humanity's greatest scandal came the announcement of unimaginable grace.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus reigns.
And sinners can still come home.
So if His voice is reaching you through these words…
do not merely admire the message.
Answer Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come out of hiding.
Follow Christ.
And when He restores you, do not bury the testimony.
Tell somebody where grace found you.
Share what Christ has done.
Point another wounded sinner toward the Savior.
Because maybe the person who “won't listen” today…
will remember the truth tomorrow.
Maybe the person resisting Jesus right now will someday become the person telling everyone else how Jesus rescued them.
Ezekiel could not see every consequence of his obedience.
Neither can you.
So speak truth.
Love people.
Pray.
Stay faithful.
Leave the results with God.
And never forget this:
The voice you keep resisting may be the mercy you will someday thank God He never stopped sending after you.
